items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The frequency of the waves received by an observer, which differs from the emitted frequency when there is relative motion along the line joining source and observer"?
items.answer: observed frequency
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of observed frequency.

items.stem: A loudspeaker emits a steady note while moving relative to an observer. Predict and explain the effect on the observed frequency if the source moves away at the same speed instead of approaching.
items.answer: the observed frequency is lower than the emitted frequency (f′ = fv/(v + u))
items.markingKey: the observed frequency is lower than the emitted frequency (f′ = fv/(v + u)) (A1 for the prediction, R1 for the reasoning in terms of wavefronts or relative motion).

items.stem: Nia is revising the Doppler effect for sound waves: moving source and moving observer. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The pitch of an approaching siren rises steadily as it gets closer.
A blueshift shows that the source is getting hotter.
Redshift means the galaxy looks red.
Loudness change is due to distance; the Doppler effect is the change in frequency (pitch), which stays higher throughout the approach.
items.answer: Loudness change is due to distance; the Doppler effect is the change in frequency (pitch), which stays higher throughout the approach.
items.markingKey: D. The other options are common misconceptions. Loudness change is due to distance; the Doppler effect is the change in frequency (pitch), which stays higher throughout the approach.

items.stem: A racing car engine note emits sound of frequency 480 Hz while approaching a stationary observer at 12 m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 330 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency heard.
items.answer: 498 Hz

items.stem:
A loudspeaker emitting a fixed frequency is carried on a track towards a microphone at different speeds u. The observed frequency f′ is recorded. Theory: 1/f′ = 1/f − u/(fv), speed of sound v = 340 m s⁻¹.

u / m s⁻¹ | f′ / Hz
5 | 812
10 | 824
15 | 836
20 | 851
25 | 863
30 | 878

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the emitted frequency f (from the y-intercept, using v from the gradient as a check). [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±2 %. State the emitted frequency with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) 1/f′ (y) against u (x); (b) gradient ≈ −3.71 × 10⁻⁶ s² m⁻¹; (c) 800 Hz; (d) 800 Hz ± 20 Hz
items.markingKey: (a) 1/f′ (y) against u (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ −3.71 × 10⁻⁶ s² m⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) f = 1/(y-intercept) = 800 Hz (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 2 % of the value = 20 Hz; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: Describe how you could use a smartphone recording of a passing car’s horn to estimate the car’s speed. Include the measurements, the equations and the main sources of uncertainty.
items.answer: Record the horn as the car approaches and recedes; use a frequency-analysis app to find f₁ (approaching) and f₂ (receding); u = v(f₁ − f₂)/(f₁ + f₂) with v ≈ 340 m s⁻¹ (adjusted for temperature). Uncertainties: frequency resolution of the app, car not moving directly along the line of sight, speed changes, wind, temperature-dependent v.
items.markingKey: Record the horn as the car approaches and recedes; use a frequency-analysis app to find f₁ (approaching) and f₂ (receding); u = v(f₁ − f₂)/(f₁ + f₂) with v ≈ 340 m s⁻¹ (adjusted for temperature). Uncertainties: frequency resolution of the app, car not moving directly along the line of sight, speed changes, wind, temperature-dependent v.

items.stem: An observer moves towards a stationary source. The observed frequency increases because
options: the speed of sound in air increases
the wavelength in the air decreases
the observer meets wavefronts more often
items.answer: the observer meets wavefronts more often
items.markingKey: C. The wavelength is unchanged; the relative speed of the waves past the observer increases.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "Doppler effect".
items.answer: The change in observed frequency (and wavelength) of a wave when the source and the observer move relative to each other
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the change in observed frequency (and wavelength) of a wave when the source and the observer move relative to each other. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a moving observer and a moving source.
items.answer: A moving source changes the wavelength of the waves in the medium (λ′ = (v ∓ u_s)/f); a moving observer leaves the wavelength unchanged but meets wavefronts at a different rate (relative speed v ± u_o).
items.markingKey: A moving source changes the wavelength of the waves in the medium (λ′ = (v ∓ u_s)/f); a moving observer leaves the wavelength unchanged but meets wavefronts at a different rate (relative speed v ± u_o). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why a moving observer and a moving source do not have exactly symmetrical Doppler formulae for sound.
items.answer: For sound there is a medium: a moving source changes the wavelength in the air, whereas a moving observer changes the speed of the waves relative to themselves with the wavelength unchanged; the two effects give different formulae.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: For sound there is a medium: a moving source changes the wavelength in the air, whereas a moving observer changes the speed of the waves relative to themselves with the wavelength unchanged; the two effects give different formulae. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A whistle is whirled in a horizontal circle. A distant observer in the plane of the circle hears a note whose frequency
items.answer: rises and falls periodically
items.markingKey: D. The line-of-sight velocity alternates between towards and away.

items.stem: "The speed of sound increases in front of a moving source." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The speed of sound depends only on the medium; it is the wavelength that decreases in front of the source.
items.markingKey: The speed of sound depends only on the medium; it is the wavelength that decreases in front of the source. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A train sounds its horn while approaching a station at constant speed. A passenger on the platform hears a frequency that
options: falls steadily as the train approaches
is constant and higher, then drops as the train passes
is constant and equal to the emitted frequency
rises steadily as the train approaches
items.answer: is constant and higher, then drops as the train passes
items.markingKey: B. Constant velocity gives a constant shift.

items.stem: A source of frequency 900 Hz moves towards a stationary observer at 17 m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency is observed?
items.answer: 947 Hz
items.markingKey: D. f′ = fv/(v − u) = 947 Hz. Using the observer formula or the wrong sign gives the distractors.

items.stem: A source of frequency 900 Hz moves towards a stationary observer at 20 m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency is observed?
items.answer: 956 Hz
items.markingKey: D. f′ = fv/(v − u) = 956 Hz. Using the observer formula or the wrong sign gives the distractors.

items.stem: A police car siren emits 700 Hz while moving at 35 m s⁻¹ (speed of sound 330 m s⁻¹). Calculate the wavelength of the sound in front of the source and behind it.
items.answer: 0.421 m in front; 0.521 m behind
items.markingKey: λ_front = (v − u)/f = 0.421 m (A1); λ_behind = (v + u)/f = 0.521 m (A1); M1 for the idea that the source moves u/f between wavefronts.

items.stem: An ambulance siren emits sound of frequency 480 Hz while approaching a stationary observer at 12 m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 343 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency heard.
items.answer: 497 Hz

items.stem: A student claims: "The pitch of an approaching siren rises steadily as it gets closer." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: For a source approaching at constant speed along the line of sight, the observed frequency is constant (and higher); it drops suddenly as it passes.
items.markingKey: For a source approaching at constant speed along the line of sight, the observed frequency is constant (and higher); it drops suddenly as it passes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A source of frequency 1000 Hz moves towards a stationary observer at 40 m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency is observed?
items.markingKey: D. f′ = fv/(v − u) = 1130 Hz. Using the observer formula or the wrong sign gives the distractors.

items.stem: A bat flying at 6.0 m s⁻¹ towards a wall emits ultrasound at 40.0 kHz (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). (a) Calculate the frequency received by the wall. (b) The wall reflects this as a stationary source; calculate the frequency the bat hears. (c) Explain how the bat could use the difference to judge its speed relative to the wall.
items.answer: (a) 40.0 × 340/334 = 40.7 kHz; (b) 40.72 × 346/340 = 41.4 kHz; (c) the frequency shift (≈ 1.4 kHz) depends on the speed of approach: Δf ≈ 2fu/v, so a larger shift means faster closing speed.
items.markingKey: Moving source formula (M1) 40.7 kHz (A1); moving-observer formula for the reflection (M1) 41.4 kHz (A1); interpretation of Δf ∝ u (R1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "A stationary observer can always tell whether a source or the observer is moving from the Doppler shift alone."
items.answer: Only for sound at appreciable speeds and with careful measurement; generally the shift alone is ambiguous.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: for sound the two cases give slightly different formulae. Arguments against: at low speeds the difference is tiny and within measurement uncertainty; wind complicates the medium frame; for light there is no difference in principle. Supported judgement: Only for sound at appreciable speeds and with careful measurement; generally the shift alone is ambiguous. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "redshift z".
items.answer: The fractional change in wavelength, z = Δλ/λ₀, which for v ≪ c is approximately v/c
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the fractional change in wavelength, z = Δλ/λ₀, which for v ≪ c is approximately v/c. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about Doppler effect for light: redshift and blueshift is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Mei.)
options: The speed of sound depends only on the medium; it is the wavelength that decreases in front of the source.
Redshift means the galaxy looks red.
For a source approaching at constant speed along the line of sight, the observed frequency is constant (and higher); it drops suddenly as it passes.
It uses the frequency shift of the echo, proportional to the speed of the blood cells along the beam.
items.answer: Redshift means the galaxy looks red.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: Redshift means that all spectral lines are shifted towards longer wavelengths; the galaxy need not appear red.

items.stem: Which statement about the Doppler effect for light is correct?
options: It changes the speed of light
It depends on the relative velocity of source and observer along the line of sight
It only occurs for visible light
items.answer: It depends on the relative velocity of source and observer along the line of sight
items.markingKey: B. No medium; c is invariant.

items.stem: A student claims: "Redshift means the galaxy looks red." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Redshift means that all spectral lines are shifted towards longer wavelengths; the galaxy need not appear red.
items.markingKey: Redshift means that all spectral lines are shifted towards longer wavelengths; the galaxy need not appear red. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A distant galaxy recedes from Earth at 9.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. Calculate the observed wavelength of its hydrogen-beta line (laboratory wavelength 486.1 nm).
Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Redshift measurements alone are enough to determine the distances of galaxies."
items.answer: Redshift gives distance only through a calibrated Hubble constant and a cosmological model.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Hubble’s law d = v/H₀ converts redshift to distance. Arguments against: H₀ must be calibrated with independent distances (Cepheids, supernovae); peculiar velocities distort nearby galaxy redshifts; at high z relativistic and cosmological models are needed. Supported judgement: Redshift gives distance only through a calibrated Hubble constant and a cosmological model.

items.stem: Light from opposite edges of the rotating Sun shows
options: a blueshift on one edge and a redshift on the other
items.answer: a blueshift on one edge and a redshift on the other
items.markingKey: A. One limb approaches, the other recedes.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The increase in observed wavelength (decrease in frequency) of light from a source moving away from the observer"?
items.answer: redshift
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of redshift.

items.stem: Distinguish between blueshift and redshift.
items.answer: Redshift is an increase in wavelength from a receding source; blueshift is a decrease in wavelength from an approaching source.
items.markingKey: Redshift is an increase in wavelength from a receding source; blueshift is a decrease in wavelength from an approaching source. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the Doppler shift of light depends only on relative velocity, unlike sound.
items.answer: Light needs no medium and its speed is the same for all observers, so there is no distinction between source and observer motion; only their relative velocity matters.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Light needs no medium and its speed is the same for all observers, so there is no distinction between source and observer motion; only their relative velocity matters. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Redshift means the galaxy looks red." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Redshift means that all spectral lines are shifted towards longer wavelengths; the galaxy need not appear red.
items.markingKey: Redshift means that all spectral lines are shifted towards longer wavelengths; the galaxy need not appear red. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how spectral lines allow astronomers to measure the speed of a distant galaxy along the line of sight.
items.answer: Elements in the galaxy produce absorption lines at known laboratory wavelengths; comparing observed and laboratory wavelengths gives Δλ/λ ≈ v/c, so v is found from the shift; redshift means recession.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Elements in the galaxy produce absorption lines at known laboratory wavelengths; comparing observed and laboratory wavelengths gives Δλ/λ ≈ v/c, so v is found from the shift; redshift means recession. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A spectral line from a binary star periodically splits into two lines and recombines. This is because
options: the two stars alternately approach and recede along the line of sight
the light is diffracted by dust
items.answer: the two stars alternately approach and recede along the line of sight
items.markingKey: A. Orbital motion gives opposite Doppler shifts.

items.stem: The calcium H line (396.8 nm) in a galaxy’s spectrum is observed at 397.59 nm. What is the recession speed of the galaxy?
The sodium D line (589.0 nm) in a galaxy’s spectrum is observed at 591.94 nm. What is the recession speed of the galaxy?
Calculate the change in frequency of the calcium H line (396.8 nm) in light from a star in a nearby galaxy moving away at 8.00 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.
items.answer: decrease of 2.02 × 10¹² Hz
items.markingKey: f = c/λ = 7.56 × 10¹⁴ Hz (A1); Δf = f v/c = 2.02 × 10¹² Hz (A1), a decrease (A1).

items.stem: The magnesium b line (517.3 nm) in a galaxy’s spectrum is observed at 522.47 nm. What is the recession speed of the galaxy?
"A blueshift shows that the source is getting hotter." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Blueshift indicates motion towards the observer; temperature is found from the spectrum’s peak (Wien’s law), not from line shifts.
items.markingKey: Blueshift indicates motion towards the observer; temperature is found from the spectrum’s peak (Wien’s law), not from line shifts. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Light from a distant galaxy shows the hydrogen-alpha line at 669.4 nm (laboratory 656.3 nm). (a) Calculate the galaxy’s recession speed. (b) Taking H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, estimate its distance. (c) Explain one reason why this distance estimate may be inaccurate.
items.answer: (a) z = 13.1/656.3 = 0.0200, v = zc = 5.99 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹; (b) d = v/H₀ = 5990/70 = 86 Mpc; (c) peculiar motion within its cluster, uncertainty in H₀, or measurement of the line centre.
items.markingKey: (a) z = 13.1/656.3 = 0.0200, v = zc = 5.99 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹; (b) d = v/H₀ = 5990/70 = 86 Mpc; (c) peculiar motion within its cluster, uncertainty in H₀, or measurement of the line centre.

items.stem: A spiral galaxy is viewed edge-on. The hydrogen-beta line (486.1 nm) is observed at 489.697 nm from one edge and 488.984 nm from the opposite edge. (a) Determine the speed of the galaxy as a whole. (b) Determine the rotation speed of the outer edge. (c) Outline how such measurements provide evidence for dark matter.
items.answer: (a) 2.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ receding; (b) 2.20 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; (c) rotation speeds stay high at large radii, implying more mass than the visible matter
items.markingKey: Mean wavelength gives the systemic shift: v = c(λ̄ − λ₀)/λ₀ = 2.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (M1 A1); half the difference gives rotation: v = cΔλ/(2λ₀) = 2.20 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (M1 A1); flat rotation curves → unseen mass (R1).

items.stem: A spiral galaxy is viewed edge-on. The hydrogen-beta line (486.1 nm) is observed at 491.285 nm from one edge and 490.637 nm from the opposite edge. (a) Determine the speed of the galaxy as a whole. (b) Determine the rotation speed of the outer edge. (c) Outline how such measurements provide evidence for dark matter.
items.answer: (a) 3.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ receding; (b) 2.00 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; (c) rotation speeds stay high at large radii, implying more mass than the visible matter
items.markingKey: Mean wavelength gives the systemic shift: v = c(λ̄ − λ₀)/λ₀ = 3.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (M1 A1); half the difference gives rotation: v = cΔλ/(2λ₀) = 2.00 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (M1 A1); flat rotation curves → unseen mass (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A device that emits microwaves at a moving vehicle and finds its speed from the Doppler shift of the reflected waves"?
items.answer: radar speed gun
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of radar speed gun.

items.stem: Tomás is revising applications: radar speed measurement and astronomical motion. Which of the following statements is correct?

Doppler ultrasound measures blood flow speed from how loud the echo is.
The pitch of an approaching siren rises steadily as it gets closer.

items.stem: A radar emits 10 GHz microwaves towards a vehicle approaching at 25 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency shift of the reflected wave?
items.markingKey: B. Δf = 2fv/c = 1670 Hz; forgetting the factor 2 gives half this value.

items.stem: An exoplanet survey detects a Sun-like star whose spectral lines shift by ±1.2 × 10⁻⁴ nm at 656 nm with a period of 4.2 days. (a) Determine the star’s radial-velocity amplitude. (b) Explain what the period tells us. (c) Discuss why this method favours finding massive planets close to their stars.
items.answer: (a) v = cΔλ/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸ × 1.2 × 10⁻⁴/656 = 55 m s⁻¹; (b) the orbital period of the planet; (c) heavier, closer planets pull the star more strongly, giving larger, faster wobbles that are easier to detect within a short survey.
items.markingKey: (a) v = cΔλ/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸ × 1.2 × 10⁻⁴/656 = 55 m s⁻¹; (b) the orbital period of the planet; (c) heavier, closer planets pull the star more strongly, giving larger, faster wobbles that are easier to detect within a short survey.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Doppler ultrasound".
items.answer: A medical technique that measures the speed of blood flow from the frequency shift of ultrasound reflected by moving blood cells

items.stem: In Doppler ultrasound, why is the shift of the reflected wave doubled?
options: the blood cells act first as a moving observer, then as a moving source
the ultrasound travels twice as fast
items.answer: the blood cells act first as a moving observer, then as a moving source
items.markingKey: A. Reception and re-emission both introduce a shift.

items.stem: Why do radar speed guns use microwaves rather than visible light?
options: microwaves do not reflect from cars
microwaves pass through rain and fog and are easily generated and detected electronically
items.answer: microwaves pass through rain and fog and are easily generated and detected electronically
items.markingKey: B. Practical generation, detection and weather penetration.

items.stem: Explain why a radar speed gun measures the beat frequency rather than the reflected frequency directly.
items.answer: The shift (hundreds or thousands of hertz) is tiny compared with the emitted frequency (~10¹⁰ Hz); mixing reflected and emitted waves produces beats at the difference frequency, which can be measured precisely.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The shift (hundreds or thousands of hertz) is tiny compared with the emitted frequency (~10¹⁰ Hz); mixing reflected and emitted waves produces beats at the difference frequency, which can be measured precisely. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how the Doppler effect is used to detect exoplanets by the radial-velocity method.
items.answer: A planet and its star orbit their common centre of mass; the star’s velocity along our line of sight oscillates, so its spectral lines shift periodically to red and blue; the period gives the orbital period and the amplitude gives the planet’s minimum mass.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A planet and its star orbit their common centre of mass; the star’s velocity along our line of sight oscillates, so its spectral lines shift periodically to red and blue; the period gives the orbital period and the amplitude gives the planet’s minimum mass. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ultrasound of frequency 5.0 MHz is directed at blood flowing at 0.60 m s⁻¹, at 0° to the flow. The speed of sound in tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency shift of the echo (Δf = 2fv cos θ/c_s).

Alessia tested a radar speed gun by measuring the speed of a car driven past at a nominally constant speed several times. The 5 readings of the measured speed were 14.8, 14.7, 15.7, 15.7, 15.0 m s⁻¹. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.markingKey: Mean = 15.2 m s⁻¹ (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.5 m s⁻¹ (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.5/15.2 × 100 = 3.3 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty.

items.stem: Ultrasound of frequency 2.0 MHz is directed at blood flowing at 0.25 m s⁻¹, at 45° to the flow. The speed of sound in tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency shift of the echo (Δf = 2fv cos θ/c_s).
items.answer: 459 Hz

items.stem: Leila checked the precision of a hand-held Doppler radar by repeating measurements on a cyclist on a velodrome. The 5 readings of the measured speed were 12.5, 13.1, 12.3, 12.2, 13.1 m s⁻¹. items.markingKey: Mean = 12.6 m s⁻¹ (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.5 m s⁻¹ (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.5/12.6 × 100 = 3.6 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty.

items.stem: Evaluate the use of the Doppler radial-velocity method for discovering Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars.
items.answer: Strengths: it measures the star’s line-of-sight wobble and gives the orbital period and minimum planet mass; it has found hundreds of planets. Limitations: an Earth-mass planet at 1 AU makes the Sun wobble by only ~0.1 m s⁻¹, requiring extreme spectrometer stability; stellar activity (spots, granulation) mimics signals; it gives only m sin i unless the inclination is known; long periods need years of data. Judgement: excellent for giant and close-in planets; for Earth analogues it needs combination with transit observations.
items.markingKey: States the principle (A1); strength with physics (R1); size of the effect quantified or explained (R1); two limitations (R1 R1); supported judgement (A1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Radar speed guns are completely reliable evidence of speeding."
items.answer: Reliable when correctly calibrated and used, but procedural safeguards are needed.

Arguments against: cosine error from aiming angle (reads low); reflections from other vehicles or moving fans; calibration must be checked regularly. Supported judgement: Reliable when correctly calibrated and used, but procedural safeguards are needed. The decrease in observed wavelength of light from a source moving towards the observer
items.answer: The frequency of the periodic variation in intensity when two waves of slightly different frequency superpose; equal to their frequency difference
items.markingKey: A. "beat frequency" is the frequency of the periodic variation in intensity when two waves of slightly different frequency superpose; equal to their frequency difference.

items.stem: Explain, using wavefronts, why the pitch of a siren is higher as it approaches and lower as it moves away.
items.answer: The source moves between emitting successive wavefronts, so in front they are closer together (shorter λ, higher f) and behind further apart (longer λ, lower f); the wave speed in air is unchanged, so the observed frequency changes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The source moves between emitting successive wavefronts, so in front they are closer together (shorter λ, higher f) and behind further apart (longer λ, lower f); the wave speed in air is unchanged, so the observed frequency changes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A teacher in Dubai asks a class to choose the one correct statement about Doppler effect for light: redshift and blueshift. Which statement should be chosen?
options: A radar gun measures speed using the time for the echo to return.
The siren gets louder as it approaches, and that is what the Doppler effect means.
Redshift means the galaxy looks red.
Redshift means that all spectral lines are shifted towards longer wavelengths; the galaxy need not appear red.
items.answer: Redshift means that all spectral lines are shifted towards longer wavelengths; the galaxy need not appear red.
items.markingKey: D. The other options are common misconceptions. Redshift means that all spectral lines are shifted towards longer wavelengths; the galaxy need not appear red.

items.stem: "A radar gun measures speed using the time for the echo to return." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The speed gun uses the frequency (Doppler) shift of the reflected wave; timing gives distance, not speed directly.
items.markingKey: The speed gun uses the frequency (Doppler) shift of the reflected wave; timing gives distance, not speed directly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A loudspeaker emits a steady note while moving relative to an observer. Predict and explain the effect on the observed frequency if the observer moves towards the source instead of the source moving towards the observer at the same speed.
items.answer: the observed frequency is still higher, but slightly less than when the source moves (the formulae differ for sound)
items.markingKey: the observed frequency is still higher, but slightly less than when the source moves (the formulae differ for sound) (A1 for the prediction, R1 for the reasoning in terms of wavefronts or relative motion).

items.stem: Explain why the redshift of distant galaxies supports the idea that the universe is expanding.
items.answer: Almost all distant galaxies show redshifts, and the redshift increases with distance (Hubble’s law); this is consistent with space itself expanding, so every galaxy moves away from every other.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Almost all distant galaxies show redshifts, and the redshift increases with distance (Hubble’s law); this is consistent with space itself expanding, so every galaxy moves away from every other. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A star shows a periodic radial-velocity variation of 50 m s⁻¹. Doubling the planet’s mass (same orbit) would make the variation approximately
items.answer: 100 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: C. The star’s wobble is proportional to planet mass for small planets.

items.stem: A source of frequency 900 Hz moves towards a stationary observer at 40 m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency is observed?
items.markingKey: C. f′ = fv/(v − u) = 1020 Hz. Using the observer formula or the wrong sign gives the distractors.

items.stem: The hydrogen-alpha line has a laboratory wavelength of 656.3 nm. In the spectrum of a radio galaxy it is observed at 657.09 nm. Determine the speed of a radio galaxy along the line of sight and state whether it is approaching or receding.
items.answer: 3.60 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, receding
items.markingKey: Δλ = 0.788 nm (A1); v = cΔλ/λ₀ (M1) = 3.60 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (A1); redshift → receding (R1).

items.stem: A radar emits 24 GHz microwaves towards a vehicle approaching at 30 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency shift of the reflected wave?
items.markingKey: C. Δf = 2fv/c = 4800 Hz; forgetting the factor 2 gives half this value.

items.stem: As a train horn passes a stationary observer, the frequency heard falls from 1074 Hz to 867.9 Hz. The speed of sound is 330 m s⁻¹. Determine the speed of the source and the emitted frequency.
items.markingKey: f₁ = fv/(v − u), f₂ = fv/(v + u) (M1); f₁/f₂ = (v + u)/(v − u) (M1); u = v(f₁ − f₂)/(f₁ + f₂) = 35.0 m s⁻¹ (A1); f = f₁(v − u)/v = 960 Hz (A1).

items.stem: A galaxy in the Virgo cluster recedes from Earth at 3.60 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Calculate the observed wavelength of its hydrogen-beta line (laboratory wavelength 486.1 nm).

Chloé tested a radar speed gun by measuring the speed of a car driven past at a nominally constant speed several times. The 5 readings of the measured speed were 14.2, 14.2, 14.7, 14.5, 14.7 m s⁻¹. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.markingKey: Mean = 14.5 m s⁻¹ (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.2 m s⁻¹ (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.2/14.5 × 100 = 1.7 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty.

items.stem: Sofia writes: "The speed of sound increases in front of a moving source." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The speed of sound depends only on the medium; it is the wavelength that decreases in front of the source.
items.markingKey: The speed of sound depends only on the medium; it is the wavelength that decreases in front of the source. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Measured redshifts prove that the universe began in a Big Bang."
items.answer: Redshifts are strong evidence for expansion and, with other evidence, support the Big Bang, but science provides support rather than proof.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: systematic redshift with distance indicates expansion; combined with the CMB and abundances of light elements it strongly supports the Big Bang model. Arguments against: redshift alone shows expansion, not a beginning; other evidence is needed; models can be revised (NOS); local galaxies (e.g. Andromeda) show blueshift. Supported judgement: Redshifts are strong evidence for expansion and, with other evidence, support the Big Bang, but science provides support rather than proof.

items.stem: "The Doppler effect is the most important tool in modern astronomy." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: It is one of the most powerful tools, but astronomy relies on several complementary methods.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: measures radial velocities, rotation, binary orbits, exoplanets and cosmic expansion. Arguments against: parallax, photometry and spectroscopy of composition and temperature are equally essential; only gives line-of-sight velocity. Supported judgement: It is one of the most powerful tools, but astronomy relies on several complementary methods. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: "A stationary observer can always tell whether a source or the observer is moving from the Doppler shift alone." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Only for sound at appreciable speeds and with careful measurement; generally the shift alone is ambiguous.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: for sound the two cases give slightly different formulae. Arguments against: at low speeds the difference is tiny and within measurement uncertainty; wind complicates the medium frame; for light there is no difference in principle. Supported judgement: Only for sound at appreciable speeds and with careful measurement; generally the shift alone is ambiguous. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: A spiral galaxy is viewed edge-on. The hydrogen-alpha line (656.3 nm) is observed at 663.344 nm from one edge and 662.382 nm from the opposite edge. (a) Determine the speed of the galaxy as a whole. (b) Determine the rotation speed of the outer edge. (c) Outline how such measurements provide evidence for dark matter.
items.answer: (a) 3.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ receding; (b) 2.20 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; (c) rotation speeds stay high at large radii, implying more mass than the visible matter
items.markingKey: Mean wavelength gives the systemic shift: v = c(λ̄ − λ₀)/λ₀ = 3.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (M1 A1); half the difference gives rotation: v = cΔλ/(2λ₀) = 2.20 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (M1 A1); flat rotation curves → unseen mass (R1).

items.stem: What happens to the wavelength in front of a moving sound source?
items.answer: it decreases
items.markingKey: B. λ′ = (v − u_s)/f.

items.stem: For a galaxy receding at speed v ≪ c, the fractional change in wavelength of its spectral lines is approximately
items.answer: v/c
items.markingKey: B. Δλ/λ ≈ v/c.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Doppler ultrasound"?
options: The decrease in observed wavelength of light from a source moving towards the observer
The change in observed frequency (and wavelength) of a wave when the source and the observer move relative to each other
A medical technique that measures the speed of blood flow from the frequency shift of ultrasound reflected by moving blood cells
The fractional change in wavelength, z = Δλ/λ₀, which for v ≪ c is approximately v/c
items.answer: A medical technique that measures the speed of blood flow from the frequency shift of ultrasound reflected by moving blood cells
items.markingKey: C. "Doppler ultrasound" is a medical technique that measures the speed of blood flow from the frequency shift of ultrasound reflected by moving blood cells.

items.stem: A student in Lisbon is checking notes on the Doppler effect for sound waves: moving source and moving observer. Which statement is incorrect?
options: The siren gets louder as it approaches, and that is what the Doppler effect means.
Blueshift indicates motion towards the observer; temperature is found from the spectrum’s peak (Wien’s law), not from line shifts.
For a source approaching at constant speed along the line of sight, the observed frequency is constant (and higher); it drops suddenly as it passes.
Redshift means that all spectral lines are shifted towards longer wavelengths; the galaxy need not appear red.
items.answer: The siren gets louder as it approaches, and that is what the Doppler effect means.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: Loudness change is due to distance; the Doppler effect is the change in frequency (pitch), which stays higher throughout the approach.

items.stem: Distinguish between redshift and blueshift.
items.answer: Redshift is an increase in wavelength from a receding source; blueshift is a decrease in wavelength from an approaching source.
items.markingKey: Redshift is an increase in wavelength from a receding source; blueshift is a decrease in wavelength from an approaching source. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

Redshift means that all spectral lines are shifted towards longer wavelengths; the galaxy need not appear red.

items.stem: A loudspeaker emits a steady note while moving relative to an observer. Predict and explain the effect on the observed frequency if a strong wind blows from the source towards a stationary observer, with neither moving.

items.stem: A speed camera emits 10.50 GHz microwaves. The beat frequency between the emitted and reflected waves from an approaching car is 2100 Hz. The speed limit is 20 m s⁻¹. Determine whether the car is speeding.
items.answer: v = 30.0 m s⁻¹; speeding
items.markingKey: v = cΔf/(2f) (M1) = 30.0 m s⁻¹ (A1); compare with 20 m s⁻¹ (R1).

items.stem:
A loudspeaker emitting a fixed frequency is carried on a track towards a microphone at different speeds u. The observed frequency f′ is recorded. Theory: 1/f′ = 1/f − u/(fv), speed of sound v = 340 m s⁻¹.

u / m s⁻¹ | f′ / Hz
5 | 811
10 | 823
15 | 837
20 | 849
25 | 864
30 | 878

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the emitted frequency f (from the y-intercept, using v from the gradient as a check). [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±5 %. State the emitted frequency with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) 1/f′ (y) against u (x); (b) gradient ≈ −3.77 × 10⁻⁶ s² m⁻¹; (c) 799 Hz; (d) 799 Hz ± 40 Hz

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Redshift measurements alone are enough to determine the distances of galaxies."
items.answer: Redshift gives distance only through a calibrated Hubble constant and a cosmological model.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Hubble’s law d = v/H₀ converts redshift to distance. Arguments against: H₀ must be calibrated with independent distances (Cepheids, supernovae); peculiar velocities distort nearby galaxy redshifts; at high z relativistic and cosmological models are needed. Supported judgement: Redshift gives distance only through a calibrated Hubble constant and a cosmological model.

items.stem: "Doppler ultrasound is safer than X-ray imaging for monitoring blood flow in pregnancy." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Yes for this purpose, because it avoids ionising radiation, provided intensity guidelines are followed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ultrasound is non-ionising; gives real-time velocity information. Arguments against: heating at high intensity must be limited; image quality depends on operator and angle of insonation; cannot image through bone or gas. Supported judgement: Yes for this purpose, because it avoids ionising radiation, provided intensity guidelines are followed. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: A train sounding a 600 Hz horn travels at 30 m s⁻¹ along a straight track; a cyclist rides at 8.0 m s⁻¹ towards the approaching train (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). (a) Calculate the frequency the cyclist hears. (b) Calculate the frequency after the train has passed, both still moving at the same speeds. (c) Explain why the frequency drop is not instantaneous for a listener standing beside the track.
items.answer: (a) f′ = 600 × (340 + 8)/(340 − 30) = 674 Hz; (b) f′ = 600 × (340 − 8)/(340 + 30) = 538 Hz; (c) the source’s velocity component along the line of sight changes gradually as the train passes, so the frequency falls smoothly over a short time.
items.markingKey: (a) f′ = 600 × (340 + 8)/(340 − 30) = 674 Hz; (b) f′ = 600 × (340 − 8)/(340 + 30) = 538 Hz; (c) the source’s velocity component along the line of sight changes gradually as the train passes, so the frequency falls smoothly over a short time.
